newsitem.title: USA: Congress might alter plan to stop Yellowstone mine.
newsitem.headline: Congress might alter plan to stop Yellowstone mine.

text.p: Congress was likely to approve a plan to stop Crown Butte from mining near Yellowstone National Park, but wants to change the proposal, government and environmental officials said on Friday.
The company must respond by April 11 to a $65 million offer the Clinton administration made last month to ban the mine, stemming from a campaign pledge by the president.

While lawmakers in both parties want the company out, several questioned the buyout and the plan for offsetting it by temporarily trimming the Conservation Reserve Programme, which pays farmers not to plant on fragile land.
Environmental officials expect Crown Butte to accept the proposal, which must then be approved by Congress. The House Resources Committee has scheduled a hearing on it next week.
Crown Butte spokesman Les Van Dyke said the company was still looking at the plan, but added that the cash offer "is the type of asset we were looking for ... something that would be liquid."

"We're confident that the deal will be executed," said Mike Clark, executive director of the Greater Yellowstone Coalition, which worked closely with the company and the government to bring about the agreement.

To balance the $65 million payment to Crown Butte, which would come from federal mineral royalties, the Clinton administration proposed to delay enrolling two million acres into the conservation reserve.

"I don't know if the CRP is going to be the offset, but if it's not, they'll find something else," Clark said, after meeting with congressional aides. "A lot of people have said they don't want to see CRP raided."
No one named specific alternatives, but the administration was open to ideas to replace the CRP delay.
"Certain aspects (of the plan) might be improved" as Congress debates the agreement, a White House official said.

The administration was trying to make clear to farm state lawmakers that its CRP plan would only involve delaying for one year the enrollment of two million out of up to 19 million acres in the reserve, not eliminating the two million acres.
Some lawmakers also questioned the wisdom of paying off the company with mineral royalties that would have gone into the Treasury.
"It is just taking it out of the Treasury," said Sen. Craig Thomas of Wyoming, who was one of the first Republicans to oppose the gold, silver and copper complex.

"The other risk is that each time someone has a claim on land of that kind, they're going to initiate some activity for the prospect of being bought out for cash. It sets a precedent that could be very difficult," Thomas told Reuters.
He said the administration should have stuck to its original idea of exchanging land or federal buildings with the company.
The White House chose the cash payment instead because it ran into problems in various states when it tried to identify property worth trading, green groups said.
